business-cycles-s1.title: Real GDP and potential output in Country X over ten quarters

plot.label: Line chart of real GDP and potential output in Country X over ten quarters (invented data)

table.caption: Country X, billions of dollars (invented data for practice)

business-cycles-s2.title: A slowdown in Halvet
business-cycles-s2.text: In Halvet, households and firms cut back on spending. For two quarters in a row real GDP falls, stores report weak sales and factories cut shifts. The unemployment rate rises from 4.5% to 7.0%. Economists estimate Halvet's natural rate of unemployment at 4.5%.

business-cycles-s3.title: A boom in Berovia
business-cycles-s3.text: Berovia's economy is booming. Firms are running extra shifts and paying overtime, and some workers have put off retiring to take well-paid jobs. The unemployment rate is 3.0%, while the natural rate is estimated at 5.0%. Prices are rising faster each month.

business-cycles-s4.title: A shift of Country W's production possibilities curve

items.q: In which quarter does Country X reach a peak?
options: Quarter 4
Quarter 10
Quarter 7
Quarter 9

why.correct: A peak is the turning point where an expansion ends and a contraction begins.
options: Right: real GDP rises to 108 in Quarter 4 and falls afterward, so Quarter 4 is the turning point at the top.
Real GDP is 108 again in Quarter 10, but it is still rising at the end of the data; there is no turning point yet.
Quarter 7 is the lowest point, the trough.
Real GDP is still rising in Quarter 9, which is part of an expansion.

items.q: Between which quarters is Country X in a contraction?
options: From Quarter 4 to Quarter 7
From Quarter 1 to Quarter 4
From Quarter 7 to Quarter 10
From Quarter 1 to Quarter 10

why.correct: The business cycle has two phases, expansion and contraction; the peak and the trough are the turning points between them.
options: Right: real GDP falls from 108 to 101 between the peak and the trough.
Real GDP rises from 100 to 108 then: an expansion.
Real GDP rises from 101 to 108 then: the next expansion.
The whole period has both an expansion and a contraction.

items.q: What is the output gap in Quarter 7, in billions of dollars? (Use a negative number if output is below potential.)

why.correct: Output gap = real GDP - potential output $= 101 - 106 = -5$ billion dollars: a negative (recessionary) gap.

mistakes.why: The size is right but the sign is wrong. Output gap = actual real GDP minus potential output, and actual is below potential here.
Quarter 7 is the lowest point, but the gap compares real GDP with potential output: $101 - 106$.

items.q: In Quarter 4, real GDP is 108 and potential output is 103. Which statement describes the economy then?
options: There is a positive (inflationary) gap, and unemployment is below its natural rate
There is a negative gap, and unemployment is above its natural rate
There is no gap, because it is the peak
There is a positive gap, and unemployment is above its natural rate

why.correct: A positive output gap goes with unemployment below the natural rate and rising inflation; a negative gap goes with cyclical unemployment.
options: Right: output above potential means firms are stretching their workers, so unemployment is below the natural rate and inflation tends to rise.
Output is above potential, so the gap is positive, not negative.
A peak is a turning point in real GDP; the gap compares real GDP with potential output.
Producing more than potential takes more workers, so unemployment is below, not above, the natural rate.

items.q: What most likely happens to cyclical unemployment in Country X from Quarter 4 to Quarter 7?
options: It rises as real GDP falls below potential
It falls as real GDP falls
It stays at zero, because potential output keeps growing
It rises, because potential output falls

why.correct: In a contraction, output falls and cyclical unemployment rises. In an expansion the reverse happens.
options: Right: firms produce less, need fewer workers and lay some off.
Less output means fewer workers are needed, so unemployment rises.
Potential output grows, but actual output falls below it: that gap is cyclical unemployment.
Potential output keeps rising in the data; it is actual output that falls.

items.q: Which phase of the business cycle is Halvet in?
options: A contraction
An expansion
A peak
Full employment

why.correct: A contraction is a period of falling real GDP. When it is severe and lasting it is called a recession.
options: Right: real GDP is falling and unemployment is rising.
In an expansion real GDP rises; here it is falling.
A peak is a single turning point, and Halvet has been falling for two quarters.
Unemployment is 7.0%, well above the 4.5% natural rate.

items.q: What is Halvet's cyclical unemployment rate now?

why.correct: Cyclical = actual - natural $= 7.0 - 4.5 = 2.5\%$.

mistakes.why: You added the actual and natural rates. Cyclical unemployment is the actual rate minus the natural rate.
That is the actual rate. Subtract the natural rate to find the cyclical part.

items.q: How does Halvet's real GDP now compare with its potential output?
options: It is below potential: a negative (recessionary) output gap
It is above potential: a positive output gap
It equals potential, because the natural rate is 4.5%
It can't be compared without knowing prices

why.correct: Cyclical unemployment and a negative output gap are two views of the same thing: the economy is producing below its full-employment output.
options: Right: unemployment above the natural rate means the economy is producing less than it could at full employment.
A positive gap goes with unemployment below the natural rate, not above it.
Output equals potential when the actual rate equals the natural rate; here it is higher.
The unemployment rates are enough: cyclical unemployment means output is below potential.

items.q: What kind of output gap does Berovia have?
options: A positive (inflationary) output gap
A negative (recessionary) output gap
No output gap, because the economy is growing
A negative gap, because prices are rising

why.correct: Unemployment below the natural rate means the economy is producing beyond its potential output for now.
options: Right: unemployment is below the natural rate, so real GDP is above potential output.
A negative gap comes with unemployment above the natural rate.
Growing output can be above, at or below potential; here it is above.
Rising prices point the other way: they come with a positive gap.

items.q: How can Berovia produce more than its potential output?
options: By running workers and machines harder for a while
By having more workers than the adult population
By counting the same output twice in the GDP figures
By moving to a point outside its PPC

why.correct: Potential output is what the economy produces at the natural rate of unemployment. Above it, firms and workers are stretched, which can last only for a while.
options: Right: potential is the sustainable full-employment level; extra shifts and overtime can push output above it temporarily.
The labor force can't exceed the adult population; output rises because people work more hours.
GDP counts final goods once; the extra output is real production.
A point outside the PPC can't be reached with current resources; a boom stretches how hard they are used.

items.q: Why are prices in Berovia rising faster each month?
options: Firms are short of workers and capacity, so they raise wages and prices
Cyclical unemployment is high, so firms raise prices
Output is below potential, so goods are scarce
The natural rate has risen to 5.0%

why.correct: Near the peak of an expansion, when output is above potential, inflation tends to rise; in a contraction it tends to slow.
options: Right: with output above potential, spending runs ahead of what firms can easily produce, and inflation tends to rise.
Unemployment is below the natural rate; there is no cyclical unemployment.
Output is above potential here.
The natural rate is given as 5.0%; nothing says it rose, and that would not raise prices each month.

items.q: The graph shows Country W's production possibilities curve shifting out over a decade. Which event could cause this shift?
options: More workers and better technology
A recession that leaves factories idle
A boom in which firms pay overtime
A rise in the inflation rate

why.correct: The PPC shows what the economy can produce with full use of its resources, so it shifts out when resources or technology grow: potential output rises.
options: Right: more resources or better technology let the economy produce more of both goods, so the PPC and potential output grow.
A recession moves production to a point inside the PPC; the curve itself does not move.
A boom pushes output above potential for a while; it does not add resources.
Faster price increases do not add workers, capital or technology.

items.q: What does the shift in the graph show about Country W's potential output?
options: It increased
It decreased
It stayed the same, because just the curve moved
It can't be told from a PPC

why.correct: Potential output corresponds to the PPC: producing on the curve is full employment, and an outward shift is growth in potential output.
options: Right: an outward PPC shift means the economy can produce more at full employment.
A decrease would be an inward shift of the curve.
The curve is what the economy can produce at full employment; when it moves out, potential output rises.
Points on the PPC are full-employment output, so its shift shows the change in potential.

items.q: Before the shift, Country W was in a recession with high cyclical unemployment. Where was it producing compared with the original PPC?
options: At a point inside the original curve
At a point on the original curve
At a point outside the original curve
On the new curve, because of the shift

why.correct: A recession is a point inside the PPC; the economy at full employment is on it; growth in potential output shifts the curve out.
options: Right: idle workers and machines mean output below what the economy could produce.
On the curve means full employment; a recession has cyclical unemployment.
Points outside the curve can't be reached with the resources the economy had.
The new curve shows later, larger potential; in the recession it was below even the old one.

items.q: Country W is in a deep recession: factories sit idle and many workers cannot find jobs. Mark a point on its PPC graph that shows where it is producing.

why.correct: Idle workers and machines mean the economy produces less than it could: a point inside the PPC.

items.q: Country W recovers until real GDP equals its potential output and unemployment equals its natural rate. Mark a point on its PPC graph that shows where it is producing now.

why.correct: At potential output the economy is at full employment and uses its resources efficiently, so it produces on the PPC.

items.q: Put the parts of one business cycle in order, starting at a peak.
options: Peak
Contraction
Trough
Expansion

why.correct: From a peak, output falls in a contraction to a trough, then rises in an expansion toward the next peak. The phases are expansion and contraction; peak and trough are the turning points.

items.q: What is potential output?
options: The real GDP an economy produces at full employment
The largest real GDP an economy has reached in the past
The real GDP an economy produces with zero unemployment
The real GDP at the trough of a business cycle

why.correct: Potential (full-employment) output is the sustainable level, at the natural rate of unemployment. It grows over time as the economy gains resources and better technology.
options: Right: output when unemployment is at its natural rate.
A past high may have been above potential during a boom.
Full employment leaves frictional and structural unemployment.
At a trough output is usually far below potential.

items.q: Over many decades, Country Z's real GDP rises through several expansions and contractions. Which line best describes its potential output over that time?
options: A rising trend line that real GDP moves above and below
A flat line, because potential is fixed
A line that moves up and down with each expansion and contraction
A line that stays above real GDP in each year

why.correct: Real GDP fluctuates around potential output, which follows a long-term upward trend.
options: Right: potential output grows over time, and the business cycle swings around it.
Potential grows as the labor force, capital and technology grow.
Actual real GDP swings; potential is the smoother trend.
In booms real GDP rises above potential, so the gap is sometimes positive.

items.q: Build the explanation: households and firms in Country V cut their spending sharply. Explain what happens to output and unemployment.

why.correct: Less spending means firms sell less, so they produce less and need fewer workers: real GDP falls below potential (a negative output gap) and cyclical unemployment rises.

specific.frame: Total spending ___, so real GDP ___, which creates a ___ output gap, and cyclical unemployment ___.
specific.model: Total spending falls, so firms sell less and produce less: real GDP falls below potential output, which leads to a negative (recessionary) output gap. Cyclical unemployment rises because firms need fewer workers.

spending.label: Total spending
options: falls
rises

why.1: Households and firms cut their spending, so total spending falls.

output.label: Real GDP
options: falls below potential
rises above potential

why.1: Firms sell less, so they produce less: output falls, it does not rise.

gap.label: The output gap
options: negative (recessionary)
positive (inflationary)

why.1: Output below potential is a negative gap; a positive gap is output above potential.

unemployment.label: Cyclical unemployment
options: rises
falls

why.1: Producing less takes fewer workers, so firms lay people off and cyclical unemployment rises.

items.q: Which of these usually happen during a contraction? Select all that apply.
options: Cyclical unemployment rises
Real GDP rises faster than potential output
The unemployment rate falls below the natural rate
Potential output shrinks to match real GDP

why.correct: In a contraction real GDP falls, often below potential, and cyclical unemployment rises; inflation tends to slow.
options: Right: firms produce less and lay off workers.
That describes an expansion.
That happens near the peak of a boom, not in a contraction.
Potential output keeps its trend; actual output falls below it.
